setup: Before the flappers and the stock ticker there is a forty-year hole, and nothing in this decade makes sense until it is filled. The story picks up in 1877, the year Reconstruction collapsed and the defeated white South was handed back its old ruling class, who spent the next quarter-century building Jim Crow — segregation, poll taxes, rigged literacy tests, sharecropping, lynching — while the Supreme Court blessed it in 1896. Meanwhile the rest of the country industrialized at a violent pace: the Gilded Age of railroads, steel, oil, and the giant monopoly trusts, then a Progressive reaction that produced the income tax, the Federal Reserve, woman suffrage, and Prohibition. Twenty-five million immigrants poured in, the source shifting to Catholic and Jewish southern and eastern Europe. Then a World War that made America the world's leading creditor and, at home, a surveillance state it never dismantled. That is the inheritance this chapter lays out — and the label "Roaring Twenties" is itself a sales pitch you should be suspicious of.

bridge: Chapter 1 set the table: a country that had let the freed people be forced back into Jim Crow, built the world's largest industrial machine and the inequality to match, taken in 25 million immigrants, and just won a war by becoming a surveillance state it never switched off. The war ends on November 11, 1918. The people living through these first years did not feel like they were roaring — and the brand name that would later be slapped on the decade has no room at all for what actually happened next.
setup: The armistice drops the country into chaos with no plan. The 1918 influenza pandemic is still burning, and it does what flu almost never does — kills healthy young adults — eventually taking roughly 675,000 Americans, more than died in combat in the World War, World War II, Korea, and Vietnam combined. The wartime command economy is dismantled overnight: prices jump, four million soldiers are mustered out with a bonus and a train ticket and no jobs, and wages that were frozen now buy far less. So workers strike — 1919 is the largest strike year in American history, one in five in the workforce walking out. A general strike paralyzes Seattle; the Boston police walk off and the city loots; a governor named Coolidge becomes a national figure overnight by breaking them. And in the middle of it all, the Nineteenth Amendment doubles the electorate. What this chapter settles is the mood the rest of the decade reacts against: a frightened country, and frightened countries do things they regret.

bridge: The country came out of Chapter 2 frightened: a deadly pandemic, four million workers on strike, every walkout described by the newspapers as the opening of a Bolshevik revolution. The Russian Bolsheviks really had seized power in 1917 and announced they meant to spread the revolution worldwide, and to a great many Americans the strikes, the immigrants, and a wave of bombs did not look like separate problems. They looked like the beginning. The wartime surveillance machinery built in Chapter 1 was sitting there fully assembled, waiting for a new target.
setup: This is the First Red Scare — one of the clearest cases in American history of a real but small threat inflated into a panic that did far more damage than the threat. There genuinely was a tiny movement of Italian anarchist bombers, and they genuinely killed people. The Attorney General, A. Mitchell Palmer, who wanted to be president, used that to license the Palmer Raids: mass arrests of around 6,000 suspected radicals, mostly immigrants, mostly without warrants, hundreds deported. Out of it came the seven-year drama of Sacco and Vanzetti and, in reaction, the founding of the ACLU. But 1919 was also one of the worst years of anti-Black violence in the country's history — the Red Summer, white mobs attacking Black communities across two dozen cities — climaxing two years later in Tulsa, where a white mob destroyed a prosperous Black district and the death toll was buried for fifty years. The chapter holds two terrors side by side and refuses to file the second under the first.

bridge: The Red Scare of Chapter 3 burned out fast — Palmer's predicted revolution never came, the courts pushed back, the country simply tired of fear. What it left behind was a surveillance apparatus, a young filer named Hoover who kept using it, and an electorate exhausted by three years of war, flu, strikes, and Bolshevik scares. After Woodrow Wilson, the crusading Progressive who had taken the country into the war and broken himself trying to drag it into the League of Nations, voters wanted one thing above all: for someone to make it stop.
setup: They got Warren Harding, who ran on a fuzzy promise he summed up in one word — "normalcy" — and won the largest popular-vote landslide to that point, a repudiation of the whole Progressive, internationalist, reforming temper of the previous twenty years. Harding is routinely ranked the worst president, and the simple version misses what makes him interesting: his administration held, at the same time, some of the most capable men of the era and some of the most corrupt. The capable ones set the policies the boom ran on — Andrew Mellon's tax cuts on the rich, Herbert Hoover's reinvented Commerce Department. The corrupt ones, the "Ohio Gang," sold pardons, contracts, and the government itself, climaxing in Teapot Dome, the scandal that became the decade's byword for graft. This chapter is how a decent, limited, badly-judging man presided over both the machinery of the boom and the worst corruption the country had yet seen — and then died before the bill came due.

bridge: Chapter 4 ended with Harding dead in San Francisco in August 1923, beloved at the moment of his death and just ahead of the scandals about to surface. His Treasury Secretary Mellon had begun cutting taxes on the rich, his Commerce Secretary Hoover had built the government's most dynamic agency, and his Ohio cronies had been quietly looting the rest. The death handed the presidency, at the exact moment the economy was about to take off, to the one man in the administration with no whiff of corruption on him: a silent, frugal Vermonter who had been kept so far from the action that he learned he was president by lamplight, in the middle of the night, at his father's farm.
setup: Calvin Coolidge built his entire brand on being the opposite of the previous five years — not heroic, not corrupt, not eloquent, not modern. "Silent Cal" understood that in a decade when everyone wanted government to stop doing things and let people get rich, the most popular thing a president could do was very little, very quietly. He continued Mellon's tax cuts, vetoed farm relief twice, and compressed his philosophy into the line the decade is remembered by: "the business of America is business." And the boom arrived to prove him right — between 1922 and 1929 the economy did something genuinely new in world history, the first mass consumer economy, where the gains showed up not as more food and rent but as cars, radios, and refrigerators, much of it bought on credit. This chapter establishes the shape of that boom and then sets down, once and at full length, who it left out: the farmers, the dying coal and textile regions, and Black Americans under Jim Crow — close to half the country the party never reached.

bridge: Chapter 5 sketched the boom in outline — the first mass consumer economy, where prosperity arrived as things to buy rather than just more food and rent — and promised to take it apart system by system. It also drew the line between the urban industrial America that was roaring and the farm, the mine, and the cotton field that were not, a division this chapter quietly explains: the consumer economy ran on the opposite principle from the cotton South the earlier narratives in this chain were built on. Now the machine itself, starting with the one object that explains everything.
setup: The object is the automobile, and the point is the way it was built, because the way the car was built is the way the whole consumer economy was eventually built. Henry Ford did not invent the car or the assembly line, but at his Highland Park plant in 1913 he put the pieces together at a scale nobody had managed — and then made the move that became the founding idea of mass consumption: pay the workers who build the cars enough that they can buy the cars. Five dollars a day, the worker as the market. But Ford saw it first and then stopped thinking, betting on one cheap unchanging car forever. Alfred Sloan's General Motors saw what came next — a car for every purse, the annual restyling, financing on credit — and beat Ford so decisively that even Ford had to shut down and retool. That contest decided the model the American economy has run on ever since. And then there is what the car did to the country: the suburb, zoning, the highway, an entire roadside economy, and families who would "go without clothes" before they'd give up the automobile.

bridge: Chapter 6 showed the factory side of the boom: Ford's assembly line and Sloan's GM building standardized goods in almost unlimited quantity, and Ford's radical insight that you have to pay the workers enough to buy what they make. But wages alone could not absorb all that output — in 1920 most families still could not pay cash for a car, a refrigerator, a radio, and a washing machine all at once. Something had to square that circle and turn the productive capacity into an actual consumer society. That something is less visible than the assembly line and at least as important.
setup: It was the normalization of going into debt to buy things. For most of American history consumer debt carried a moral stigma; in the twenties that stigma was deliberately dissolved through the installment plan — take it home now, pay monthly with interest, the seller keeping the right to repossess. By the late twenties most cars, radios, and appliances were bought this way, and consumer debt became a permanent structural feature of the economy. Credit gave people the money; modern advertising, much of it on Madison Avenue, gave them the wanting, learning to sell not the product but relief from a fear or a desire — Listerine inventing "halitosis" to sell mouthwash. The chain store killed the neighborhood merchant; electrification wired the urban home for the appliances. Put it together and you have the machine the whole decade ran on — and a structural fragility, a floor made of debt and confidence, that the brand version never mentions and Chapter 15 collects on.

bridge: Chapters 6 and 7 built the consumer economy — the factories that could make almost anything, the credit and wages that let ordinary people buy it, the advertising that manufactured the wanting. But a national consumer market needs a national pulpit: some way to reach tens of millions of scattered strangers with the same message at the same moment. That pulpit did not exist when the decade began. By the time it ended it had been invented, consolidated, and handed to advertisers — and it carried not only the singing commercial but the decade's argument about whose country this was.
setup: On a Pittsburgh rooftop in November 1920, station KDKA read out election returns to a few hundred listeners — conventionally the first commercial broadcast. Within the decade radio reached a third of American homes and did something never done in human history: it let millions hear the same voice, joke, and advertisement at the same instant. America made the choice to pay for it with advertising, the opposite of Britain's public BBC, and that choice rewarded the most profitable content — including demeaning imitations of Black culture. Meanwhile Hollywood consolidated into the studio system, built the movie palace, manufactured the modern celebrity and the celebrity scandal, and then, with The Jazz Singer in 1927, killed the silent era overnight — its headline act a white star in blackface, broadcasting a caricature of the very Black music being made uptown in Harlem. This chapter is the birth of the broadcast nation, and the question of whose voice it carried and whose it sold.

bridge: The earlier chapters built the roaring half of the decade — the cars, the credit, the broadcast nation. This chapter turns to the backlash half that ran on the same calendar, and it traces back to the fear of Chapter 3. The Red Scare burned out, but the postwar fusion of anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic, anti-Jewish, anti-radical, and anti-Black feeling did not. It hardened into a single political emotion that called itself "100% Americanism," and for a century the United States had kept its door, for Europeans, essentially open — about 25 million had come since 1880. In a four-year span, Congress slammed it shut.
setup: And it did so openly, on stated grounds of race and national origin, with the science of the day cited in the committee reports — this is text, not subtext. The mechanism was the quota, and the design was the whole point: the 1924 Johnson–Reed Act pegged each nation's quota to the 1890 census, deliberately reaching back to a year before the great southern- and eastern-European wave, so that Italians, Poles, Greeks, Russians, and Jews would be cut to a trickle. The arithmetic was the policy. The act also barred essentially all immigration from Japan and Asia outright, poisoning relations for a generation. The intellectual cover was eugenics — entirely mainstream, taught in universities, blessed by the Supreme Court in 1927 when it upheld forced sterilization with the line "Three generations of imbeciles are enough." Running the other way, almost in passing, the same Congress finally granted citizenship to Native Americans born in the country — which several states then quietly hollowed out. This is the pattern of rights in the decade: granted on paper, qualified in practice, never quite for everyone at once.

bridge: Chapter 9 named the decade's organizing emotion outside the cities — "100% Americanism," the fusion of anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic, anti-Jewish, anti-radical, and anti-Black feeling — and showed it written into the immigration quotas as law. But that same emotion also built a mass membership organization, and this chapter is it. The brand version of the twenties either omits it or files it under "the South." That is the single biggest thing to get right here, because it is wrong.
setup: In August 1925, tens of thousands of hooded men marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in daylight, and they were as likely to be from Indiana, Oregon, or Colorado as from Georgia. This was the second Ku Klux Klan — a different animal from the Reconstruction terror that came before and the civil-rights resistance that came after — refounded in 1915 on ground prepared by The Birth of a Nation, then mass-marketed by promoters who took a cut of every fee into a multi-million-member national fraternal organization. It sold itself not primarily as a lynching society but as a Protestant lodge, a temperance enforcer, a defender of "old-stock" Americans, which made it socially respectable — "100% Americanism" with a costume and a sales force. Its violence was real, and so was its political power: it controlled Indiana, and in 1924 one of the two major parties could not bring itself, by about one vote, to officially condemn it. Then it collapsed almost overnight, on a single sordid crime, which is one reason the decade could later be remembered as roaring rather than seething. This book does not leave it out.

bridge: The Klan of Chapter 10 loved Prohibition and styled itself its vigilante arm — and Prohibition is the next front in the same culture war, the rural Protestant America of the quotas and the lodge trying to discipline the modern, urban, immigrant, wet America the rest of this book describes. It arrived through the Progressive machinery of Chapter 1 as a constitutional amendment, and it is the strangest single choice the decade made.
setup: On January 17, 1920, the United States wrote a total nationwide ban on making, selling, and transporting alcohol into its Constitution — the only amendment ever to take a freedom away, and the only one ever repealed. No other major country went this far; America reached for the most drastic instrument available, which is exactly why it became the textbook case. It was the victory of the Anti-Saloon League, the most effective single-issue pressure group to that point, but the Volstead Act funded enforcement so feebly that the federal force never topped a couple thousand poorly paid, easily bribed agents. The result is almost a controlled experiment in the limits of law: drinking fell somewhat, especially among the poor, but mostly it went underground into speakeasies, a lethal bootleg supply chain, and — the consequence that outlived Prohibition itself — the modern organized-crime syndicate, financed and built by bootleg money. Its emblem is Al Capone, who grossed an estimated $60 million a year and owned a city, and who was finally brought down not for murder or bootlegging but for failing to file a tax return.

bridge: The Klan and Prohibition of the last two chapters were both rural Protestant America trying to hold the line against the modern, urban, scientific country this book keeps describing. This chapter stages the argument underneath all of it — the deepest fight of the decade — in the open, in front of the whole listening country, as a single contest between two famous old men in a sweltering Tennessee courthouse.
setup: American Protestantism was splitting along a fault the decade widened into a canyon: modernists, who reconciled faith with science, against fundamentalists, who insisted on the literal, inerrant truth of the Bible. The battlefield was the public school, where the state decided which account of human origins every child would be taught. Tennessee's Butler Act made it a crime to teach evolution; the ACLU advertised for a test case; Dayton boosters recruited a mild substitute teacher named John Scopes. Then the case caught fire because of who came to argue it — William Jennings Bryan for the prosecution, Clarence Darrow for the defense — and peaked when Darrow put Bryan himself on the stand and pushed him into a confused defense of biblical literalism on national radio. The urban press, led by H. L. Mencken, wrote it as a total modernist rout, and Bryan's death five days later made the legend feel complete. But the legend is the winners' version, written in real time, and this chapter takes it apart: the modernists won the press and lost the country.

bridge: Chapter 5 promised that the farm crisis and a great migration north were one story, not two — both the failure of Reconstruction's broken land promise finally cashing out, sixty years deferred. Chapters 9 and 10 showed the decade's politics, the quotas and the Klan, trying to suppress exactly the Americans this chapter is about. Now those threads converge in a few square miles of upper Manhattan and the South Side of Chicago, where the most lasting thing the Roaring Twenties made was being created — by the people the rest of the decade was built to keep down.
setup: It starts with the Great Migration: between 1916 and 1930, more than 1.5 million Black Americans left the rural South for Northern and Midwestern cities, the largest internal migration in American history to that point — pushed by Jim Crow, debt, and lynching, pulled by wartime and post-1924 labor shortages and the smuggled Chicago Defender. That concentration produced an explosion with three wings. The literary one, the Harlem Renaissance, had its manifesto in Alain Locke's The New Negro and its voices in Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, and Claude McKay. The political one ran in parallel — Marcus Garvey's mass movement, the NAACP's anti-lynching fight strangled by the Senate filibuster, A. Philip Randolph's porters' union. But the musical wing reached the most people fastest, carried by the new machines of Chapter 8, and one man — Louis Armstrong — turned a regional folk music into a fine art almost single-handedly. The chapter ends in the Cotton Club, the decade in one room: the greatest Black artists performing for a whites-only audience, entering through the back.

bridge: Chapter 13 told the cultural story the decade tried to suppress — the Black art that became its most lasting legacy. This chapter tells the cultural story the decade told about itself: the Jazz Age, the flapper, the famous writers, the manufactured heroes. They are not the same as the brand suggests either. The advertising of Chapter 7 was telling the country it had never been happier; the decade's best young writers were saying, in the country's best prose, that the boom was spiritually empty and the optimism was a fraud.
setup: F. Scott Fitzgerald, famous at twenty-three, coined "the Jazz Age" and wrote The Great Gatsby — which sold modestly and became "the great American novel" only later, itself a lesson in how the decade was remembered versus lived. He and the rest are the decade's internal dissent: Hemingway and the Lost Generation in cheap, legal-wine Paris, Mencken warring daily on the "booboisie" at home. The decade's emblem of social change was the flapper — bobbed hair, public cigarettes, the Charleston — and there was something real underneath the image, but the brand sells the image as the reality: she was largely an urban, young, white, middle-class figure and substantially a media construction, and the vote had not delivered economic or legal equality. Held against the dissenters was the decade's last invention, the modern celebrity manufactured at industrial scale — Babe Ruth, Gertrude Ederle, and above all Charles Lindbergh, fame itself turned into an industry. The dissenters and the manufactured heroes are the decade arguing with itself, and the machine had the bigger circulation.

bridge: Every chapter has been pointing here. The consumer economy of Chapters 6 and 7 ran on borrowing against the future; the same logic, applied to stocks, ends the decade. Coolidge walked out the door in 1927 before the bill arrived (Chapter 5) and handed the boom, and the Crash, to Herbert Hoover, the admired engineer of Chapters 4 and 5. The boom was real and narrow and borrowed, and almost nobody with the power to say so would — because the entire system, the credit, the advertising, the politics, the market, depended on no one saying it.
setup: The decade ends in a crowd of ordinary people who had borrowed against a future they were certain would arrive, discovering over about eleven days in October 1929 that it would not. There was a dress rehearsal — the Florida land mania of 1923–1925 — that taught the wrong lesson, and the speculative money simply moved north to the New York Stock Exchange. The mechanism was the same borrowing-against-the-future logic as the installment plan: buying on margin (ten percent down, ninety percent borrowed) and the leveraged investment trust, both of which magnified gains on the way up and guaranteed cascading forced selling on the way down. A few warned and were mocked; the experts who reassured were believed; the Federal Reserve, caught between popping the bubble and crushing the real economy, dithered. The Dow peaked September 3, slid for seven weeks, then broke — Black Thursday, Black Monday, and Black Tuesday's roughly 16 million shares. The book stops at the cliff edge: the Crash triggered but did not, by itself, cause the Great Depression, which is the next story's to tell.
